stem: The meeting was cancelled because the manager was ill.
options: The manager's illness led to the cancellation of the meeting.
The manager became ill during the meeting.
The meeting was held without the manager, who was ill.
The manager cancelled the meeting and then became ill.
solutionSteps: Identify the causal direction: illness caused the cancellation.
Check the order of events: he was ill first, then the meeting was cancelled.
Option 1 preserves both the cause and the order.

trapExplanations.1: Places the illness during the meeting, but the original says the meeting never happened.
trapExplanations.2: Says the meeting took place, contradicting 'was cancelled'.
trapExplanations.3: Reverses the order — the original makes illness the cause, not the consequence.

stem: Few students passed the exam on their first attempt.
options: Most students needed more than one attempt to pass the exam.
No student passed the exam on the first attempt.
Most students passed the exam on their first attempt.
The exam could only be taken once.
solutionSteps: 'Few' means a small number, but not zero.
If few passed first time, the majority did not — they needed another attempt.
Option 1 states exactly that.

trapExplanations.1: 'Few' is not 'none' — some students did pass. This is the classic quantifier trap.
trapExplanations.2: Reverses the meaning entirely.
trapExplanations.3: Adds a rule about retakes that the original never mentions.

stem: Unless you register by Friday, you will not be able to attend the workshop.
options: Registering by Friday is required in order to attend the workshop.
If you register by Friday, you will definitely attend the workshop.
Registration closes after the workshop begins.
Everyone who attends the workshop registered on Friday.
solutionSteps: 'Unless X, not Y' means X is necessary for Y.
Necessary is not the same as sufficient — registering makes attendance possible, not certain.
Option 1 says 'required', which is exactly necessity.

trapExplanations.1: Turns a necessary condition into a sufficient one — 'definitely' overstates the original.
trapExplanations.2: Invents a timing detail that is not in the sentence.
trapExplanations.3: Says everyone registered exactly on Friday, but the original allows registering earlier.

stem: The proposal, while economically sound, was politically unacceptable.
options: The proposal made economic sense but could not be accepted politically.
The proposal was rejected because it was economically weak.
The proposal was acceptable both economically and politically.
Politicians agreed with the proposal despite its economic flaws.
solutionSteps: 'While X, Y' sets up a concession: X is granted, Y is the problem.
X = economically sound (positive), Y = politically unacceptable (negative).
Option 1 keeps both halves with the same polarity.

trapExplanations.1: Reverses the economics — the original grants that it was sound.
trapExplanations.2: Drops the political objection entirely.
trapExplanations.3: Inverts both halves: politicians agreeing, economics flawed.

stem: Not all of the allegations were substantiated.
options: Some of the allegations were not supported by evidence.
None of the allegations were supported by evidence.
All of the allegations were false.
The allegations were all proven true.
solutionSteps: 'Not all' negates the universal claim, leaving a partial one.
It means at least one was unsubstantiated — but not necessarily all.
Option 1 says 'some ... not', which is exactly the negation of 'all'.

trapExplanations.1: 'Not all' is not 'none'. This is the single most common restatement trap on the test.
trapExplanations.2: Overstates in the same direction as option 1, and adds a falsity claim.
trapExplanations.3: Reverses the meaning completely.

stem: The company only began investing in safety after the accident occurred.
options: Before the accident, the company had not invested in safety.
The accident happened because the company invested in safety.
The company invested in safety in order to prevent the accident.
The company stopped investing in safety once the accident occurred.
solutionSteps: 'Only began ... after X' places the start of the action strictly after X.
That entails nothing of the kind happened before X.
Option 1 states that entailment directly.

trapExplanations.1: Reverses cause and effect — the accident prompted the investment, not the other way round.
trapExplanations.2: Prevention would require investing before the accident, contradicting 'after'.
trapExplanations.3: Turns beginning into stopping — the opposite action.

stem: Her findings are significant not because they are surprising, but because they are so easily replicated.
options: The importance of her findings lies in their reproducibility rather than their novelty.
Her findings are both surprising and easy to replicate.
Her findings are unimportant because they are unsurprising.
Her findings would be more significant if they were surprising.
solutionSteps: 'Not because X, but because Y' rejects X as the reason and asserts Y.
X = surprising (novelty), Y = easily replicated (reproducibility).
Option 1 preserves the rejection of X and the assertion of Y.

trapExplanations.1: The original denies that the findings are surprising as the source of significance; this asserts both.
trapExplanations.2: The original affirms significance — this denies it.
trapExplanations.3: Introduces a hypothetical comparison the original never makes.

stem: Had the warning been issued earlier, the damage might have been contained.
options: The damage could possibly have been limited if the warning had come sooner.
The warning was issued early and the damage was contained.
The damage was certainly caused by the late warning.
An earlier warning would definitely have prevented all damage.
solutionSteps: 'Had X ...' is an unreal past conditional: X did not happen.
'Might have been' expresses possibility, not certainty.
Option 1 keeps both the counterfactual and the hedged possibility.

trapExplanations.1: States as fact what the original explicitly presents as contrary to fact.
trapExplanations.2: 'Certainly' overstates 'might' and turns possibility into established causation.
trapExplanations.3: 'Definitely ... all damage' doubly overstates: 'might' becomes certainty and 'contained' becomes total prevention.

stem: The regulation applies to all vehicles except those manufactured before 2010.
options: Vehicles made in 2010 or later are subject to the regulation.
Only vehicles manufactured before 2010 must follow the regulation.
The regulation applies to no vehicle manufactured after 2010.
All vehicles, regardless of age, must comply with the regulation.
solutionSteps: The rule covers everything, minus one carved-out group.
The carve-out is 'manufactured before 2010', so what remains is 2010 and later.
Option 1 describes precisely the remaining set.

trapExplanations.1: Inverts the exception — the pre-2010 vehicles are the ones excluded, not the only ones included.
trapExplanations.2: Also inverts the rule, exempting exactly the group that is covered.
trapExplanations.3: Ignores the exception clause altogether.

stem: The shop opens at nine and closes at six.
options: The shop is open for nine hours each day.
The shop is open for six hours each day.
The shop opens at six and closes at nine.
The shop is closed between nine and six.
solutionSteps: Convert to a 24-hour span: nine in the morning to six in the evening.
From 9 to 18 is nine hours.
Option 1 states that duration.

trapExplanations.1: Takes the closing hour as the duration.
trapExplanations.2: Reverses opening and closing times.
trapExplanations.3: Inverts open and closed — that is the period it is open.

stem: Everyone in the class except Maya finished the assignment.
options: Maya was the only one who did not finish.
Only Maya finished the assignment.
Nobody finished the assignment.
Maya finished before the others.
solutionSteps: 'Everyone except X' means all but X.
So the rest finished and X did not.
Option 1 states exactly that.

trapExplanations.1: Inverts the exception, making Maya the only finisher.
trapExplanations.2: Contradicts 'everyone ... finished'.
trapExplanations.3: Says Maya finished, which the exception denies.

stem: He rarely arrives on time.
options: He is usually late.
He is never late.
He always arrives on time.
He never arrives at all.
solutionSteps: 'Rarely' means seldom but not never.
If punctuality is rare, lateness is the norm.
'Usually late' preserves the frequency.

trapExplanations.1: Reverses the meaning entirely.
trapExplanations.2: Also the reverse of what is stated.
trapExplanations.3: 'Rarely on time' still means he arrives — just late.

stem: The policy was adopted despite strong opposition from the board.
options: The board objected, but the policy was adopted anyway.
The board's opposition prevented the policy.
The board supported the policy strongly.
The policy was adopted because the board objected.
solutionSteps: 'Despite X' concedes X and asserts the outcome anyway.
X is board opposition; the outcome is adoption.
Option 1 keeps both.

trapExplanations.1: 'Despite' means the opposition did not prevent it.
trapExplanations.2: Reverses the board's stance.
trapExplanations.3: Turns concession into causation — the opposition did not cause adoption.

stem: Sales rose in every region apart from the north, where they held steady.
options: Sales did not fall in any region.
Sales fell in the north.
Sales rose in every region including the north.
Sales rose only in the north.
solutionSteps: Everywhere but the north: rose. In the north: held steady.
Holding steady is neither a rise nor a fall.
So no region saw a decline.

trapExplanations.1: 'Held steady' explicitly rules out a fall. The most tempting misreading.
trapExplanations.2: Contradicts the exception for the north.
trapExplanations.3: Inverts which regions rose.

stem: No decision will be made before the report is published.
options: A decision can only come after publication of the report.
A decision will be made as soon as the report is published.
The report will be published after the decision.
No decision will ever be made.
solutionSteps: 'No X before Y' makes Y a prerequisite for X.
Publication must precede any decision.
It does not promise a decision will follow.

trapExplanations.1: Turns a necessary condition into a guarantee with a timetable.
trapExplanations.2: Reverses the order of the two events.
trapExplanations.3: The statement delays a decision, it does not rule one out.

stem: The treaty is binding on signatories only insofar as their domestic law permits.
options: Domestic law sets the limit of each signatory's obligation.
The treaty overrides the domestic law of signatories.
Signatories have no obligations under the treaty.
Domestic law must be changed to match the treaty.
solutionSteps: 'Only insofar as X permits' makes X the ceiling on the obligation.
X is domestic law.
So obligation extends exactly as far as domestic law allows, and no further.

trapExplanations.1: Exactly reverses the hierarchy the clause establishes.
trapExplanations.2: There are obligations — they are bounded, not absent.
trapExplanations.3: The clause accommodates domestic law rather than demanding it change.

stem: It is not that the method fails, but that its successes cannot be distinguished from chance.
options: The method may work, but the evidence cannot show that it does.
The method has been shown to fail.
The method succeeds more often than chance would predict.
The method works only by chance.
solutionSteps: 'Not that X, but that Y' denies X and asserts Y.
X is failure — denied. Y is indistinguishability from chance.
That is a claim about evidence, not about the method being wrong.

trapExplanations.1: Failure is precisely what the sentence denies.
trapExplanations.2: If successes exceeded chance they would be distinguishable — the opposite is stated.
trapExplanations.3: Asserts the method does not work, going beyond a claim about evidence. The strongest distractor.

stem: Far from settling the question, the new findings have multiplied the possible explanations.
options: The findings left the question more open than before.
The findings resolved the question conclusively.
The findings eliminated most competing explanations.
The findings confirmed the existing explanation.
solutionSteps: 'Far from X' asserts the opposite of X.
X is settling the question, so the question was not settled.
'Multiplied the explanations' means more openness, not less.

trapExplanations.1: Asserts exactly what 'far from' denies.
trapExplanations.2: Multiplying explanations is the opposite of eliminating them.
trapExplanations.3: Confirmation would reduce the range of explanations, not expand it.

stem: The concert was postponed because of the heavy rain.
options: Heavy rain caused the concert to be moved to a later date.
The concert went ahead despite the heavy rain.
The concert was called off and will not take place at all.
The rain stopped in time for the concert to begin.
solutionSteps: Fix the cause: rain.
Fix what happened to the concert: postponed, meaning moved later.
Only the first option keeps both the cause and the delay.

trapExplanations.1: Reverses the outcome — the concert did not go ahead.
trapExplanations.2: Postponed means delayed, not cancelled; a later date still exists.
trapExplanations.3: Contradicts the stated cause: the rain is why it was postponed.

stem: Only members are allowed to use the swimming pool.
options: Nobody who is not a member may use the pool.
All members use the swimming pool regularly.
Anyone may use the pool if a member comes with them.
Members are the only people who want to use the pool.
solutionSteps: 'Only X may' sets a restriction on who is permitted.
A restriction says who is excluded, not what people actually do.
The first option states the same exclusion in negative form.

trapExplanations.1: Being allowed to do something is not the same as doing it.
trapExplanations.2: Adds a guest rule the original never mentions.
trapExplanations.3: Swaps permission for desire — the original says nothing about wanting.

stem: She finished the report before the deadline.
options: The report was completed in time.
She missed the deadline for the report.
The deadline was extended so that she could finish.
She started work on the report before the deadline.
solutionSteps: Identify the action: finishing.
Identify its timing: earlier than the deadline.
'Completed in time' preserves both.

trapExplanations.1: States the opposite of finishing before the deadline.
trapExplanations.2: Invents an extension; the original says she simply finished early.
trapExplanations.3: Starting before a deadline says nothing about whether she finished.

stem: The shop closes earlier on Sundays than on weekdays.
options: On Sundays the shop shuts before its usual weekday hour.
The shop is closed for the whole of Sunday.
The shop opens later on Sundays than on weekdays.
The shop closes early on every day of the week.
solutionSteps: The comparison is between Sunday and weekdays.
What differs is the closing hour, and Sunday's is earlier.
The first option keeps both the day and the direction of the difference.

trapExplanations.1: Closing early is not the same as never opening.
trapExplanations.2: Changes closing time to opening time — a different part of the day.
trapExplanations.3: Removes the comparison; the original contrasts Sunday with other days.

stem: Tickets cost less if you book them online.
options: Booking online is the cheaper way to buy a ticket.
Tickets can only be bought online.
Online tickets sell out more quickly than others.
Tickets booked online are free of charge.
solutionSteps: The sentence compares two prices for the same ticket.
The online price is the lower one.
'Cheaper way to buy' states that comparison directly.

trapExplanations.1: A price advantage does not mean other channels are closed.
trapExplanations.2: Speed of selling is never mentioned in the original.
trapExplanations.3: Cheaper is not the same as costing nothing.

stem: He apologised for arriving late.
options: He said he was sorry for having come late.
He arrived on time but apologised anyway.
He was late and offered no apology.
He explained why the meeting had started late.
solutionSteps: Two facts: he was late, and he apologised.
A restatement must keep both.
The first option carries the lateness and the apology.

trapExplanations.1: Removes the lateness, which is what the apology was for.
trapExplanations.2: Removes the apology, reversing the sentence.
trapExplanations.3: Shifts the subject from his own lateness to the meeting's start.

stem: The proposal was accepted although several members had reservations.
options: Some members had doubts, but the proposal went through all the same.
The proposal was rejected because of the members' reservations.
Every member supported the proposal without hesitation.
The members' reservations were resolved before the vote was taken.
solutionSteps: 'Although' concedes something that did not prevent the outcome.
The outcome is acceptance; the concession is that doubts existed.
A correct restatement keeps both, joined by a contrast.

trapExplanations.1: Reverses the outcome — the proposal was accepted, not rejected.
trapExplanations.2: Deletes the reservations that 'although' explicitly reports.
trapExplanations.3: Adds a resolution the original never mentions; the doubts may well have remained.

stem: Few of the participants completed the questionnaire.
options: Most of the participants did not finish the questionnaire.
None of the participants completed the questionnaire.
The questionnaire was completed by most participants.
A few participants completed it, which pleased the researchers.
solutionSteps: 'Few' means a small number — and by implication most did not.
Convert the positive statement about a minority into its negative equivalent.
'Most did not finish' says the same thing from the other side.

trapExplanations.1: 'Few' is not 'none'; a small number did complete it.
trapExplanations.2: Reverses the quantity entirely.
trapExplanations.3: Adds a reaction from the researchers that the original does not report.

stem: The company will not proceed unless funding is secured.
options: Funding has to be obtained before the company can go ahead.
Once funding is secured, the company is certain to proceed.
The company will go ahead whether or not funding is found.
The company has already secured the funding it needs.
solutionSteps: 'Not X unless Y' makes Y a requirement for X.
A requirement is necessary, not automatically sufficient.
'Has to be obtained before' states the necessity without overclaiming.

trapExplanations.1: Turns a necessary condition into a guarantee — funding may be needed yet other obstacles remain.
trapExplanations.2: Removes the condition altogether, reversing the sentence.
trapExplanations.3: Asserts as fact something the original leaves open.

stem: Sales dipped slightly in the first quarter but had recovered by the summer.
options: After a small early fall, sales returned to their previous level.
Sales fell sharply and never regained their earlier level.
Sales rose steadily throughout the whole year.
Sales recovered first and then began to fall.
solutionSteps: Two stages in order: a small fall, then a recovery.
'Slightly' limits the size of the fall.
The first option keeps the size, the sequence and the recovery.

trapExplanations.1: Overstates the fall and denies the recovery the original reports.
trapExplanations.2: Erases the dip, leaving only growth.
trapExplanations.3: Reverses the order of the two stages.

stem: The results are significant only when the sample is large.
options: A large sample is needed for the results to be significant.
A large sample always makes the results significant.
The results are significant regardless of the size of the sample.
Small samples produce insignificant results in every field of study.
solutionSteps: 'Only when Y' makes Y a requirement for the claim.
Again this is necessity, not a guarantee.
'Needed for' captures the requirement exactly.

trapExplanations.1: Upgrades a requirement into a guarantee; size may be necessary without being enough.
trapExplanations.2: Deletes the condition, contradicting the original.
trapExplanations.3: Generalises to every field, a claim the sentence never makes.

stem: He rarely comments on his own work.
options: It is unusual for him to discuss what he has produced.
He never comments on his own work.
He frequently explains his work to others.
He comments only on work produced by other people.
solutionSteps: 'Rarely' means seldom, not never.
The subject of the comments is his own work.
'Unusual for him to discuss' preserves both the frequency and the subject.

trapExplanations.1: 'Rarely' allows occasional comment; 'never' does not.
trapExplanations.2: Reverses the frequency.
trapExplanations.3: Adds a claim about other people's work that the original omits.

stem: Had the warning been issued earlier, the damage might have been avoided.
options: Issuing the warning sooner could possibly have prevented the damage.
The warning was issued early and the damage was successfully avoided.
Because the warning came late, the damage was certainly unavoidable.
The damage was caused by the warning itself.
solutionSteps: This is a counterfactual: the warning was in fact not issued earlier.
'Might have' expresses possibility, not certainty.
The first option keeps both the unreal past and the hedged possibility.

trapExplanations.1: Treats the unreal condition as something that actually happened.
trapExplanations.2: Upgrades 'might' to certainty, which the hedge explicitly avoids.
trapExplanations.3: Inverts cause and effect entirely.

stem: The findings challenge, without wholly refuting, the accepted model.
options: The results cast doubt on the accepted model but do not completely overturn it.
The results completely disprove the accepted model.
The results confirm the accepted model in every respect.
The results neither support nor question the accepted model.
solutionSteps: Two forces here: challenge (against) and 'without wholly refuting' (limited).
A restatement must keep the doubt and the limit on it.
The first option carries both.

trapExplanations.1: Drops the limit; 'without wholly refuting' rules out complete disproof.
trapExplanations.2: Reverses the direction — the findings work against the model.
trapExplanations.3: Removes the challenge, leaving the model untouched.

stem: Not all of the recommendations were implemented.
options: Some of the recommendations were not put into practice.
None of the recommendations were implemented.
Every recommendation was implemented, though only in part.
All of the recommendations were formally rejected.
solutionSteps: 'Not all' negates the whole, not each one.
That leaves at least one unimplemented, and possibly some implemented.
'Some were not' is the precise equivalent.

trapExplanations.1: Negates every one, which is stronger than negating the whole.
trapExplanations.2: Shifts the negation from how many to how completely each was carried out.
trapExplanations.3: Rejection is a decision; the original only says they were not implemented.

stem: The technique is effective, provided that it is applied consistently.
options: The technique works so long as it is used in a consistent way.
The technique works even when it is applied inconsistently.
Consistency is the only advantage the technique offers.
The technique has been shown to work in every study of it.
solutionSteps: 'Provided that' introduces a condition on the claim.
The claim is effectiveness; the condition is consistent application.
'So long as' is a direct equivalent of 'provided that'.

trapExplanations.1: Deletes the condition, which is the whole point of 'provided that'.
trapExplanations.2: Turns the condition into a benefit, changing what the sentence asserts.
trapExplanations.3: Claims universal evidence the original never offers.

stem: Far from discouraging applicants, the stricter requirements attracted more of them.
options: The stricter requirements increased rather than reduced the number of applicants.
The stricter requirements put off a large number of applicants.
The number of applicants was unchanged by the stricter requirements.
Applicants were discouraged by the requirements but applied nonetheless.
solutionSteps: 'Far from X' denies X: applicants were not discouraged.
The second half gives what happened instead: more applied.
The first option denies the fall and states the rise.

trapExplanations.1: Asserts exactly what 'far from' denies.
trapExplanations.2: The original reports an increase, not stability.
trapExplanations.3: Reintroduces the discouragement the sentence rules out.

stem: Whatever its merits, the plan cannot be funded this year.
options: The plan may well be a good one, but no money is available for it this year.
The plan has no merits, and for that reason cannot be funded.
The plan will be funded next year instead.
It is the plan's merits that make funding impossible.
solutionSteps: 'Whatever its merits' sets the quality of the plan aside rather than denying it.
The refusal is about money this year, not about quality.
The first option keeps the quality open and the funding closed.

trapExplanations.1: Denies the merits, while the original deliberately leaves them open.
trapExplanations.2: Adds a promise about next year that the sentence does not make.
trapExplanations.3: Makes the merits the cause of the refusal, which reverses the concession.
